content:
Quick answer: Non-live vaccines can usually be given during immune-suppressing arthritis treatment, but suitability, NHS eligibility and timing need checking. Live vaccines may be unsafe with some medicines or doses. Ask your rheumatology team about your vaccine plan, especially with rituximab. Do not stop or delay treatment yourself.

This guide is for adults discussing vaccination while taking arthritis medicines. It is not an individual vaccine schedule. The medicine, dose, combinations, previous vaccines, allergies and other health conditions all matter.

Why vaccination matters with arthritis medicines

Some arthritis medicines suppress parts of the immune system, increasing the risk of certain infections or making them more serious. Vaccination can reduce risk, but protection is not complete. A DMARD label alone does not tell you how suppressed your immune system is or which NHS vaccines you qualify for.

Tell the vaccination team about methotrexate, leflunomide, azathioprine, mycophenolate, biologics, JAK inhibitors and steroid tablets, including doses and recent treatment. Hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are not treated in the same way as stronger immune-suppressing treatments for vaccine decisions; combinations and other conditions can change the advice. Take your full medicine list rather than deciding for yourself.

Live and non-live vaccines

  • Non-live vaccines cannot replicate and cause the infection they protect against. They can usually be given to people with weakened immune systems, in line with national recommendations. This does not remove other precautions, such as a previous serious allergic reaction. Tell the vaccinator about previous reactions so they can assess the right product and setting.
  • Live vaccines contain weakened organisms. With significant immunosuppression they can sometimes cause severe or fatal infection, so they must not be given without checking the medicine-specific advice with the appropriate specialist. Lower doses of some medicines may allow certain live vaccines; a blanket ban on every DMARD is not accurate.

Examples of live vaccines include MMR or MMRV, chickenpox, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid and the nasal spray flu vaccine. An injected flu vaccine is not live. Recent treatment can still matter after a medicine has stopped. Do not use a general waiting period from this guide to decide that a live vaccine is safe.

These principles come from UKHSA Green Book chapter 6 and chapter 7. Vaccine-specific chapters and current programme advice take precedence where programmes have changed.

Which vaccines should I ask about?

Clinical suitability and eligibility for an NHS-funded programme are different questions. The summary below uses NHS England information checked on 25 November 2026. Offers, booking routes and timing can differ across the UK and can change. Check NHS vaccination information for England, NHS inform for Scotland, Public Health Wales or nidirect for Northern Ireland, or ask your GP or vaccination service.

Injected flu vaccine

The NHS flu programme includes people whose immune system is weakened by a condition or treatment. It is offered each autumn or winter, and household contacts of people with weakened immune systems can also qualify. The injected vaccine is non-live. Protection falls over time and the vaccine is updated, so eligible people need it each year.

COVID-19

The current NHS England offer includes people aged 6 months to 74 years with a weakened immune system because of a condition or treatment, adults aged 75 or over and residents in care homes for older adults. A medicine name alone does not settle eligibility; steroid dose and other treatment details matter. These vaccines cannot give you COVID-19. Check each seasonal offer and ask whether you need an extra dose because of severe immunosuppression.

Pneumococcal vaccine

Pneumococcal vaccination protects against some bacterial infections that can cause pneumonia, meningitis or sepsis. It is offered from age 65 and to younger people in defined risk groups, including some people with weakened immune systems. It is non-live. The product and number of doses depend on risk and vaccination history; do not assume one dose covers every situation.

Shingles

Shingrix, the shingles vaccine used by the NHS, is non-live. NHS England eligibility includes people aged 18 or over with a severely weakened immune system, as well as defined older-adult groups. Not everyone taking a DMARD automatically qualifies. Eligible severely immunosuppressed adults are offered two doses, usually 8 weeks to 6 months apart. Ask your GP or rheumatology team to confirm your eligibility and timing rather than assuming that non-live means suitable for everyone.

RSV and other vaccines

Current NHS England RSV eligibility includes people aged 75 or over, people aged 65 to 74 with a weakened immune system or certain long-term lung conditions, and residents in care homes for older adults. RSV vaccination is also offered from 28 weeks of pregnancy. It is not an automatic offer to every adult taking a DMARD. Other vaccines, including hepatitis B, may be needed for particular risks; your vaccination service can check your record.

Timing before and during treatment

Ask about vaccination when a new medicine is discussed. Green Book chapter 7 says non-live vaccines should ideally be given at least two weeks before immunosuppressive treatment starts, where possible. They can still be given during treatment when needed. Live vaccines often need a longer interval and a specialist plan. Do not delay necessary treatment or a vaccination appointment on your own.

Vaccines may produce a reduced immune response during treatment. How much this matters varies by medicine and vaccine; it is not always only a slight reduction. Rituximab needs particular timing advice. Newcastle Hospitals' rheumatology advice recommends vaccination at least two weeks, ideally four weeks, before an infusion to improve response. Your own team must balance treatment urgency, infection risk and likely vaccine response. Do not reschedule an infusion yourself.

Do not stop, pause or change an arthritis medicine for a vaccine unless your rheumatology team specifically advises it. A clinician may recommend an individual timing plan; this is not a general instruction to miss methotrexate or other doses.

A minor illness without fever or systemic upset is not usually a reason to postpone vaccination. If you have a high temperature or feel acutely unwell, contact the vaccination service for advice before attending. If you feel unwell after a vaccine, do not automatically assume it is an expected side effect or ignore your medicine's infection advice.

Family and household vaccinations

Household members should keep their recommended vaccines up to date. Most routine live vaccines can be given to contacts of someone who is immunosuppressed, with vaccine-specific precautions:

  • After a baby's rotavirus vaccine, wash hands carefully after nappy changes and before preparing food or direct contact with the immunosuppressed person. Eligible babies should still receive their routine vaccination.
  • If a contact develops a blister-like rash after a chickenpox-containing vaccine, seek advice and avoid exposing the vulnerable person to the rash until it is dry and crusted. Covering a localised rash or avoiding contact may be needed.
  • Most contacts can receive the nasal spray flu vaccine. If close contact with a very severely immunosuppressed person, such as someone requiring isolation after a bone marrow transplant, is unavoidable, ask the vaccination team about an injected non-live alternative. This exception does not apply automatically to every person on a biologic.

See Green Book chapters 6 and 7 and the August 2026 influenza chapter. If you are exposed to chickenpox or measles while immunosuppressed, contact your clinical team promptly even if you feel well; do not wait for symptoms.

Travel vaccines

Get travel health advice early. NHS advice is to seek advice at least four to six weeks before travel; an individual immunosuppression plan may need longer. Tell the clinic every medicine and dose. Live travel vaccines, such as yellow fever and oral typhoid, may be unsuitable. Ask about alternatives and whether your destination is safe for you rather than changing your arthritis treatment to fit a trip.

Side effects and when to get help

Soreness, tiredness or aches can occur after vaccination. The expected symptoms and duration depend on the vaccine; use its patient leaflet. Get medical advice for worsening symptoms, symptoms that concern you or signs of infection, especially while taking immune-suppressing treatment.

For urgent non-emergency help, use your GP or clinical team's urgent advice route, or call 111 in England, Scotland or Wales. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service. Follow any specific infection or fever instructions supplied with your medicine.

Call 999 for a life-threatening emergency, including suspected anaphylaxis with sudden throat or tongue swelling, serious breathing difficulty or collapse. After a COVID-19 vaccine, chest pain or tightness, severe breathing difficulty or a fast-beating, fluttering or pounding heart need emergency assessment, as described in NHS COVID-19 vaccine advice. Do not drive yourself to A&E.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have the flu jab on methotrexate?

The injected flu vaccine is non-live and is generally recommended for people whose treatment weakens their immune system. Ask your team about your own eligibility and timing. Do not miss methotrexate doses unless your team tells you to.

Which vaccines should I avoid on biologics?

Live vaccines may be unsafe during treatment and for a period afterwards. Your specialist must check the particular medicine, dose, vaccine and timing. Non-live vaccines can usually be given, but allergies and other precautions still matter.

Can I have Shingrix on a JAK inhibitor?

Shingrix is non-live and can be used in eligible immunosuppressed adults. Ask your GP or team to confirm eligibility, suitability and the two-dose schedule. Do not assume all shingles vaccines or all treatment situations are the same.

Will vaccines still work?

The response may be reduced, particularly with some treatments such as rituximab. Your team can advise on timing and any extra doses. Vaccination does not give complete protection, so continue appropriate infection precautions.

How NICE and UK vaccination guidance fit together

NICE NG100, recommendations 1.3.1 and 1.3.2, supports understandable treatment information and shared decisions for adults with rheumatoid arthritis. It does not supply this guide's vaccine eligibility or medicine-specific schedules. Those details come from UKHSA's Green Book, current NHS programme information and individual specialist advice. A citation is not NICE approval of this article.

Educational information only, not a personal vaccine or treatment plan. Follow advice from your own vaccination and rheumatology teams.
